## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa1)

Summary:

This work contributes several important and interesting observations regarding the heterotolerance of non-growing Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa to the antimicrobial peptide tachyplesin. The primary mechanism of action of tachyplesin is thought to be disruption of the bacterial cell envelope, leading to leakage of cellular contents after a threshold level of accumulation. Although the MIC for tachyplesin in exponentially growing E. coli is just 1 ug/ml, the authors observe that a substantial fraction of a stationary phase population of bacteria survives much higher concentrations, up to 64 ug/ml. By using a fluorescently labelled analogue of tachyplesin, the authors show that the amount of per-cell intracellular accumulation of tachyplesin displays a bimodal distribution, and that the fraction of "low accumulators" correlates with the fraction of survivors. Using a microfluidic device, they show that low accumulators exclude propidium iodide, suggesting that their cell envelopes remain largely intact, while high accumulators of tachyplesin also stain with propidium iodide. They show that this phenomenon holds for several clinical isolates of E. coli with different genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance, and for a strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. However, the bimodal distribution does not occur in these organisms for several other antimicrobial peptides, or for tachyplesin in Klebsiella pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus, indicating some degree of specificity in the interaction between AMP and bacterial cell envelope. They next explore the dynamics of the fluorescent tachyplesin accumulation and interestingly show that a high degree of accumulation is initially seen in all cells, but that the "low accumulator" subpopulation manages to decrease the amount of intracellular fluorescence over time, while the "high accumulator" subpopulation continues to increase its intracellular fluorescence. Focusing on increased efflux as a hypothesised mechanism for the "low accumulator" phenotype, based on transcriptomic analysis of the two subpopulations, the authors screen putative efflux inhibitors to see if they can block the formation of the low accumulator subpopulation. They find that both the protonophore CCCP and the SSRI sertraline can block the formation of this subpopulation and that a combination of sertraline plus tachyplesin kills a greater fraction of the stationary phase cells than either agent alone, similar to the killing observed when growing cells are treated with tachyplesin.

Strengths:

This study provides new insight into the heterogeneous behaviours of non-growing bacteria when exposed to an antimicrobial peptide, and into the dynamics of their response. The single-cell analysis by FACS and microscopy is compelling. The results provide a much-needed single-cell perspective on the phenomenon of tolerance to AMPs and a good starting point for further exploration.

Weaknesses:

The authors have substantially improved the clarity of the manuscript and have added additional experiments to probe further the location of the AMP relative to low and high accumulators, and the physiological states of these sub-populations. These experiments strengthen the assertion that low accumulators keep the AMP at the cell surface while high accumulators permit intracellular access to the AMP.

The phenomenon of the emergence of low accumulators, which are phenotypically tolerant to the antimicrobial peptide tachyplesin, is interesting and important even if there is still work to be done to understand the mechanism by which it occurs.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa2)

Summary:

This study reports on the existence of subpopulations of isogenic E. coli and P. aeruginosa cells that are tolerant to the antimicrobial peptide tachyplesin and are characterized by accumulation of low levels of a fluorescent tachyplesin-NBD conjugate. The authors then set out to address the molecular mechanisms, providing interesting insights even though the mechanism remains incompletely defined: The work demonstrates that increased efflux may cause this phenotype, putatively together with other changes in membrane lipid composition. The authors further demonstrate that pharmacological manipulation can prevent the generation of tolerance. The authors are cautious in their interpretation, and the claims made are largely justified by the data.

Strengths:

Going beyond the commonly used bulk techniques for studying susceptibility to AMPs, Lee et al. used fluorescent antibiotic conjugates in combination with flow cytometry analysis to study variability in drug accumulation at the single cell level. This powerful approach enabled the authors to expose bimodal drug accumulation patterns that were condition-dependent but conserved across a variety of E. coli clinical isolates. Using cell sorting in combination with colony-forming unit assays as well as quantitative fluorescence microscopic analysis in a microfluidics setup, the authors compellingly demonstrate that low accumulators (where fluorescence signal is mostly restricted to the membrane) can survive antibiotic treatment, whereas high accumulators (with high intracellular fluorescence) were killed.

The relevance of efflux for the ‘low accumulator’ phenotype and its survival is convincingly demonstrated by the following lines of evidence: (i) A time-course experiment on tachyplesin-NBD pre-loaded cells revealed that all cells initially were high accumulators, before a subpopulation of cells subsequently managed to reduce signal intensity, demonstrating that the ‘low accumulator’ phenotype is an induced response and not a pre-existing property. I(i) Double-mutants deficient in the delta acrA delta tolC double-KO, which showed reduced levels of low accumulators. Interestingly, ‘low accumulator’ populations were nearly abrogated in bacteria deficient in the qse quorum sensing system, suggesting its centrality for the tachyplesin response. Even though this system may control acrA, the strength of the phenotype may suggest that it may control additional as-of-yet unidenitified factors relevant in the response to tachyplesin. I(ii) treatment with efflux pump inhibitor sertraline and verapamil (even though some caution needs to be taken since it is not perfectly selective, see weakness) prevents generation of low accumulators. The observation that sertraline enhances tachyplesin-based killing is an important basis for developing combination therapies.

The study convincingly illustrates how susceptibility to tachyplesin adaptively changes in a heterogeneous way dependent on the growth phases and nutrient availability. This is highly relevant also beyond the presented example of tachyplesin and similar subpopulation-based adaptive changes to the susceptibility towards antimicrobial peptides or other drugs may occur during infections in vivo and they would likely be missed by standardized in vitro susceptibility testing.

Weaknesses:

Some mechanistic questions regarding tachyplesin accumulation and survival remain. One general shortcoming of the setup of the transcriptomics experiment is that the tachyplesin-NBD probe itself has antibiotic efficacy and induces phenotypes (and eventually cell death) in the ‘high accumulator’ cells. As the authors state themselves, this makes it challenging to interpret whether any differences seen between the two groups are causative for the observed accumulation pattern of if they are a consequence of differential accumulation and downstream phenotypic effects.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.99752.4.sa3)

Summary:

This important study shows that stationary phase bacteria survive antimicrobial peptide treatment by switching on efflux pumps, generating low accumulating subpopulations that evade killing-a finding with clear implications for the design of peptide based antibiotics and for researchers studying antimicrobial resistance. The evidence is solid and frequently convincing, as diverse single-cell assays, genetics and chemical inhibition coherently link reduced intracellular peptide to survival, even though a few mechanistic details warrant further exploration.

Strengths:

The authors investigate how Escherichia coli (and, to a lesser extent, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) survive exposure to the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) tachyplesin. Because resistance to AMPs is thought to rely heavily on non genetic adaptations rather than on classical mutation-based mechanisms, the study focuses on phenotypic heterogeneity and seeks to pinpoint the cellular processes that protect a subset of cells. Using fluorescently labelled tachyplesin, single cell imaging, flow cytometry, transcriptomics, targeted genetics, and chemical perturbations, the authors report that stationary phase cultures harbor two phenotypic states: high accumulating cells that die and low accumulating cells that survive. They further propose and show that inducible efflux activity is the primary driver of survival and show that either efflux inhibition (sertraline, verapamil) or nutrient supplementation prevents the emergence of low accumulators and boosts killing.

The experiments unambiguously reveal that the cells respond to stress heterogeneously, with two distinct subpopulations - one with better survival than the other. This primary phenotype is convincingly shown across various E. coli strains, including clinical isolates. The authors probed the underlying mechanism from several angles, with important additional experiments in the revised version that strengthens the original conclusions in several ways. Newly added efflux assays with ethidium bromide, together with proteinase treatment experiments and ΔacrAΔtolC and ΔqseB/qseC mutant data, illustrate that the low-accumulating subpopulation can actively export intracellular compounds. The authors took great care to temper their language to acknowledge other potential alternatives that could explain some of the data such as altered influx, vesicle release or proteolysis, metabolic activity of the cells, an indirect effects of sertraline treatment. Additional metabolic dye measurements confirm that low accumulators are less metabolically active, and a new data on nutrient supplementation shows that forcing growth increases peptide uptake and lethality. The authors clarify the crucial point of where antimicrobial peptides actually bind on the cell within the broader survival mechanism and present their conclusions, along with potential caveats, with commendable clarity.

Weaknesses:

Despite these advances, the contribution of efflux may require more direct evidence to further dissect whether efflux is necessary, sufficient, or contributory. The facts that the key low-efflux mutant still retains a small fraction of survivors and that the inhibitors used may cause other physiological changes leading to higher efflux are still unaccounted for. The lipidomic and vesicle findings, while intriguing, remain descriptive, and direct tests of their functional relevance would further solidify the mechanistic models.

Conclusion:

Even with these limitations, the study provides valuable insight into non genetic resistance mechanisms to AMPs and highlights inducible heterogeneity as a critical obstacle to peptide therapeutics. In a much broader context, this study also underscores the importance of efflux physiology even for those antimicrobials that seemingly would not have intracellular targets.

results.result: Stationary phase E. coli BW25113 and nine clinical isolates display bimodal accumulation of tachyplesin-NBD at concentrations ≥16 μg/mL, with distinct low and high accumulator subpopulations. This bimodal distribution is also observed in P. aeruginosa but not in K. pneumoniae or S. aureus. The bimodal distribution is specific to tachyplesin-NBD and not observed with other AMPs tested (arenicin-NBD, polymyxin-B-NBD, octapeptin-NBD).
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C29 provide comprehensive flow cytometry data showing dose-dependent bimodal accumulation patterns across multiple bacterial strains and species. The data are internally consistent, include appropriate controls (untreated cells, different AMPs), and demonstrate reproducibility across clinical isolates with diverse genetic backgrounds. The specificity to certain AMPs and bacterial species strengthens the validity of the observations.

results.result: Low accumulators retain tachyplesin-NBD primarily on bacterial membranes, while high accumulators accumulate the peptide intracellularly. Low accumulators at 37°C exhibit fluorescence patterns similar to all cells treated at 0°C (where membrane transport is inhibited). High accumulators show significantly higher membrane-to-cell center fluorescence ratios (p<0.0001), and proteinase K treatment does not reduce fluorescence in high accumulators, confirming intracellular localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C38 provide multiple complementary lines of evidence (temperature controls, proteinase K digestion, microfluidics microscopy, confocal microscopy) that converge on the same conclusion about differential localization. The statistical analysis is appropriate (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.0001), and the experimental controls (0°C treatment, proteinase K) are well-designed to distinguish membrane-bound from intracellular peptide.

results.result: Low accumulators maintain membrane integrity and survive tachyplesin treatment, while high accumulators exhibit membrane damage and significantly reduced survival. Low accumulator survival is not significantly different from untreated controls, whereas high accumulator survival is significantly lower (p<0.0001). PI staining correlates strongly with tachyplesin-NBD accumulation (r²=0.70, p<0.0001), and the proportion of low accumulators correlates linearly with population survival (r²=0.98, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 demonstrate a clear mechanistic link between accumulation patterns, membrane integrity, and survival through multiple independent assays (CFU counts, PI staining, flow cytometry). The statistical analyses are robust with strong correlations and appropriate significance testing. The use of fluorescence-activated cell sorting followed by viability assays provides direct evidence linking phenotype to outcome.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis reveals 1,563 differentially expressed genes between low and high accumulators, organized into five distinct clusters. Low accumulators show downregulation of genes involved in protein synthesis, energy production, and gene expression (cluster 2), and upregulation of genes involved in organic substance transport (cluster 4), including efflux pump components (emrK, mdtM, mdtE, mdtF).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 present comprehensive transcriptomic data with appropriate statistical methods (DESeq2, edgeR, FDR correction) and clear clustering analysis. The PCA shows distinct separation between groups, and gene ontology enrichment provides biological context. However, the authors acknowledge that these transcriptomic differences could be either causative or consequential, which is an important limitation that prevents stronger mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: Low accumulators display transcriptomic and lipidomic changes consistent with multiple resistance mechanisms: downregulation of clsB (cardiolipin synthase), dramatic reduction in phosphatidylglycerol (37% to 3%), differential expression of genes associated with OMV secretion (ompA, ompC, degP, mcrB, tolA, tolB, pal downregulated; nlpA, lysS, waaC, waaF upregulated), and upregulation of peptidases and proteases.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 integrate transcriptomic and lipidomic data to identify multiple potential resistance mechanisms. The lipidomic analysis using UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS provides quantitative evidence for membrane composition changes that align with transcriptomic predictions. The identification of genes associated with OMV secretion and proteolytic activity is supported by appropriate citations to prior literature establishing these connections.

results.result: Transcription factor activity inference identifies 126 TFs with differential activity between low and high accumulators. Among the top ten TFs with higher activity in low accumulators, four regulate transport systems: Nac, EvgA, Cra, and NtrC.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 use computational inference (VIPER) to predict TF activities from gene expression data, which is an indirect measure. While the analysis is methodologically sound and uses established tools, the authors explicitly state that 'further experiments should be carried out to directly measure the activity of these TFs.' Without direct experimental validation, these remain computational predictions rather than demonstrated findings.

results.result: Time-course analysis reveals that the entire E. coli population initially accumulates tachyplesin-NBD to high levels (median 15,000 a.u. at 15 min), but a subpopulation subsequently reduces intracellular accumulation (median 3,600 a.u. at 60 min) while the other subpopulation continues to accumulate the drug (median increasing from 15,000 to 32,000 a.u. over 120 min).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 provide critical kinetic data demonstrating that low accumulation is an induced response rather than a pre-existing phenotype. The time-course measurements are well-controlled and show clear temporal dynamics. This finding is important for distinguishing between different mechanisms of phenotypic resistance and is supported by multiple time points with consistent trends.

results.result: Deletion of efflux pump components (ΔacrAΔtolC) or quorum sensing regulators (ΔqseB, ΔqseBΔqseC) dramatically reduces or eliminates low accumulators. The ΔqseB and ΔqseBΔqseC mutants display only high accumulators, while ΔacrAΔtolC shows reduced numbers of low accumulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 and C90 provide direct genetic evidence linking efflux systems to the low accumulator phenotype. The use of gene deletion mutants is appropriate, and the results are consistent with the known roles of AcrAB-TolC in AMP resistance (supported by citations C69). The complete elimination of low accumulators in qseBC mutants provides strong evidence for the regulatory role of this two-component system.

results.result: Efflux pump inhibitors sertraline (30 μg/mL) and verapamil (50 μg/mL) prevent the emergence of low accumulators. Sertraline cotreatment with tachyplesin-NBD increases both intracellular accumulation and PI-stained cells, and reduces survival by fivefold compared to tachyplesin-1 alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 and C102 demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of efflux pumps prevents the low accumulator phenotype and enhances tachyplesin efficacy. The experiments include appropriate controls (sertraline alone shows no effect on survival) and multiple readouts (accumulation, PI staining, CFU counts). However, C103 notes an important limitation: the sertraline concentration used exceeds clinically achievable plasma levels, which limits immediate translational potential.

results.result: Low tachyplesin-NBD accumulators display lower metabolic activity as measured by resorufin fluorescence, while high accumulators display high resorufin fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 uses resazurin reduction as a proxy for metabolic activity, but the experimental design includes CCCP to minimize efflux differences. However, CCCP disrupts multiple cellular processes beyond efflux, and the authors acknowledge that 'some variability in efflux may still persist.' The correlation between low accumulation and low metabolism is interesting but requires additional validation with alternative metabolic assays to confirm this is not an artifact of differential efflux of resorufin itself.

results.result: Nutrient supplementation (glucose and casamino acids) or exponential growth phase prevents the emergence of low accumulators and enhances tachyplesin efficacy. Stationary phase cells in nutrient-supplemented M9 show unimodal high accumulation (median 35,000 a.u.), and exponential phase cells show minimal low accumulators (10% vs 43% in stationary phase).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 demonstrate that metabolic state influences the low accumulator phenotype. The experiments compare multiple conditions (stationary vs exponential phase, with/without nutrients) and show consistent effects on both accumulation patterns and survival. This provides important context for understanding when the phenotype emerges and suggests metabolic interventions as potential therapeutic strategies, though the authors appropriately note limitations of nutrient supplementation in clinical contexts.

results.result: There is a strong correlation between tachyplesin intracellular accumulation and efficacy. After initial homogeneous accumulation, tachyplesin is retained intracellularly by non-surviving bacteria and only on membranes of surviving bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (accumulation kinetics, localization studies, survival assays, PI staining) to establish the central finding of the paper. The correlation is supported by quantitative data (r²=0.98 between low accumulator proportion and survival, r²=0.70 between accumulation and PI staining). This represents a well-supported mechanistic model linking accumulation, localization, and outcome.

results.result: This study reports the first observation of phenotypic resistance to tachyplesin within isogenic E. coli and P. aeruginosa populations, characterized by bimodal accumulation patterns. Low accumulators emerge subsequent to initial high accumulation, demonstrating upregulation of MFS, ABC, and RND efflux pumps with enhanced survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 and C89-C91 establish the novelty and significance of the findings. The claim of 'first observation' is supported by the absence of prior reports in the cited literature. The characterization is comprehensive, including accumulation patterns, transcriptomics, genetic validation, and survival data. The demonstration that low accumulators emerge after initial high accumulation (C91) is particularly important for establishing this as an induced response rather than pre-existing heterogeneity.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis reveals upregulation of the arn operon in low accumulators, which is involved in biosynthesis and attachment of positively charged L-Ara4N to lipid-A.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 identifies a specific mechanism (LPS modification) that could reduce tachyplesin binding. The transcriptomic evidence is supported by appropriate citation (Yan et al., 2007) establishing the function of the arn operon. This finding aligns with the known mechanism of AMP resistance through charge modification of the outer membrane, though direct measurement of L-Ara4N levels would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The QseBC two-component system plays an important role in controlling tachyplesin efflux. ΔqseBΔqseC mutants display only high accumulators, and QseBC was previously inferred to mediate resistance to tachyplesin analogues by upregulating efflux genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 provide both genetic evidence (deletion mutants) and literature support (Yu et al., 2020) for the role of QseBC in tachyplesin resistance. The complete elimination of low accumulators in the double mutant is striking and suggests QseBC is necessary for the phenotype. However, the authors appropriately note that QseBC deletion may have pleiotropic effects beyond efflux regulation, and the mechanism may involve regulation of AcrA/TolC or other components.

results.result: Background claims establishing the context for AMR, AMPs, tachyplesin properties, mechanisms of AMP action and resistance, and prior work on phenotypic resistance and efflux.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C16, C23, C81-C83, C86-C88, C92-C93, C95-C98, C101, C103-C106) provide essential background and context through citations to established literature. They are appropriately referenced and accurately represent prior work. These are standard background claims that frame the research question and interpret the findings in context of existing knowledge.

results.result: Stationary phase E. coli populations treated with tachyplesin-NBD display a bimodal distribution of drug accumulation, with distinct low and high accumulator subpopulations. This bimodal pattern is observed across multiple E. coli clinical isolates and P. aeruginosa, but not in K. pneumoniae or S. aureus, and varies with different AMPs.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'identify a subpopulation of cells that evade lethal damage by limiting the intracellular accumulation.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the amount of per-cell intracellular accumulation of tachyplesin displays a bimodal distribution' and that this 'holds for several clinical isolates of E. coli...and for a strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the bimodal drug accumulation patterns that were condition-dependent but conserved across a variety of E. coli clinical isolates.'

results.result: Low accumulators retain tachyplesin-NBD primarily on the cell membrane, while high accumulators accumulate the drug intracellularly. This is demonstrated through temperature-dependent accumulation, proteinase K resistance, membrane-to-cell center fluorescence ratios, and confocal microscopy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding with the added experiments. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors have substantially improved the clarity of the manuscript and have added additional experiments to probe further the location of the AMP relative to low and high accumulators...These experiments strengthen the assertion that low accumulators keep the AMP at the cell surface while high accumulators permit intracellular access to the AMP.' Reviewer 3 notes 'proteinase treatment experiments...illustrate that the low-accumulating subpopulation can actively export intracellular compounds' and praises how 'The authors clarify the crucial point of where antimicrobial peptides actually bind on the cell.'

results.result: Low accumulators survive tachyplesin treatment and maintain membrane integrity (no PI staining), while high accumulators are killed and show membrane damage (PI positive). The proportion of low accumulators strongly correlates with population survival (r²=0.98).
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this key finding. Reviewer 1 states 'The study provides compelling evidence that reduced drug accumulation underlies the decreased susceptibility of this subpopulation to the AMP.' Reviewer 2 notes 'low accumulators exclude propidium iodide, suggesting that their cell envelopes remain largely intact, while high accumulators of tachyplesin also stain with propidium iodide' and that 'the fraction of "low accumulators" correlates with the fraction of survivors.' Reviewer 3 confirms the authors 'compellingly demonstrate that low accumulators (where fluorescence signal is mostly restricted to the membrane) can survive antibiotic treatment, whereas high accumulators (with high intracellular fluorescence) were killed.'

results.result: Time-course experiments reveal that all cells initially accumulate high levels of tachyplesin-NBD within 15 minutes, but a subpopulation subsequently reduces intracellular accumulation over time (becoming low accumulators), while others continue to accumulate the drug. This demonstrates that the low accumulator phenotype is an induced response rather than a pre-existing state.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this temporal finding. Reviewer 2 states 'They next explore the dynamics of the fluorescent tachyplesin accumulation and interestingly show that a high degree of accumulation is initially seen in all cells, but that the "low accumulator" subpopulation manages to decrease the amount of intracellular fluorescence over time, while the "high accumulator" subpopulation continues to increase its intracellular fluorescence.' Reviewer 3 notes 'A time-course experiment on tachyplesin-NBD pre-loaded cells revealed that all cells initially were high accumulators, before a subpopulation of cells subsequently managed to reduce signal intensity, demonstrating that the "low accumulator" phenotype is an induced response and not a pre-existing property.'

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis of sorted low and high accumulators reveals differential gene expression patterns. Low accumulators show upregulation of efflux pump genes (MFS and RND components like emrK, mdtM, mdtE, mdtF), transport-related transcription factors, and genes associated with OMV secretion and peptidases. They also show downregulation of genes involved in protein synthesis, energy production, and cardiolipin synthesis (clsB), with corresponding changes in membrane lipid composition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support the transcriptomic findings while noting interpretive limitations. Reviewer 3 states 'The relevance of efflux for the "low accumulator" phenotype and its survival is convincingly demonstrated' and notes the transcriptomic data as part of the evidence. However, Reviewer 3 also cautions 'One general shortcoming of the setup of the transcriptomics experiment is that the tachyplesin-NBD probe itself has antibiotic efficacy and induces phenotypes...this makes it challenging to interpret whether any differences seen between the two groups are causative for the observed accumulation pattern or if they are a consequence.' The authors acknowledge this limitation in their interpretation.

results.result: Genetic deletion studies show that ΔqseB and ΔqseB/ΔqseC mutants display only high accumulators with no low accumulator subpopulation, while ΔacrA/ΔtolC mutants show reduced numbers of low accumulators. This implicates the QseBC quorum sensing system and AcrAB-TolC efflux pump in the low accumulator phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these genetic findings. Reviewer 3 states 'Double-mutants deficient in the delta acrA delta tolC double-KO...showed reduced levels of low accumulators. Interestingly, "low accumulator" populations were nearly abrogated in bacteria deficient in the qse quorum sensing system, suggesting its centrality for the tachyplesin response.' The reviewer notes 'the strength of the phenotype may suggest that it may control additional as-of-yet unidentified factors relevant in the response to tachyplesin,' acknowledging both the support and remaining mechanistic questions.

results.result: Efflux pump inhibitors sertraline and verapamil prevent the emergence of low accumulators, increase tachyplesin-NBD accumulation and PI staining, and enhance bacterial killing. Combination treatment with sertraline and tachyplesin results in fivefold lower survival compared to tachyplesin alone.
results.evaluation: All reviewers support this finding while noting caveats about inhibitor specificity. Reviewer 2 states 'both the protonophore CCCP and the SSRI sertraline can block the formation of this subpopulation and that a combination of sertraline plus tachyplesin kills a greater fraction of the stationary phase cells than either agent alone.' Reviewer 3 notes 'treatment with efflux pump inhibitor sertraline and verapamil...prevents generation of low accumulators. The observation that sertraline enhances tachyplesin-based killing is an important basis for developing combination therapies,' though adds '(even though some caution needs to be taken since it is not perfectly selective).' Reviewers acknowledge the authors' careful interpretation of potential indirect effects.

results.result: Low accumulators display lower metabolic activity (resorufin fluorescence) compared to high accumulators. Nutrient supplementation or exponential phase growth conditions prevent or reduce the emergence of low accumulators and enhance tachyplesin efficacy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these findings as important additions. Reviewer 3 states 'Additional metabolic dye measurements confirm that low accumulators are less metabolically active, and a new data on nutrient supplementation shows that forcing growth increases peptide uptake and lethality.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The study convincingly illustrates how susceptibility to tachyplesin adaptively changes in a heterogeneous way dependent on the growth phases and nutrient availability. This is highly relevant also beyond the presented example of tachyplesin.'

results.result: This study reports the first observation of phenotypic resistance to tachyplesin within isogenic E. coli and P. aeruginosa populations, characterized by a bimodal distribution of accumulation. There is a strong correlation between tachyplesin intracellular accumulation and efficacy, with surviving bacteria retaining the drug only on membranes while killed bacteria accumulate it intracellularly.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the novelty and importance of this finding. Reviewer 1 calls it 'This important study' that 'explores the heterogeneous response of non-growing bacteria to the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) tachyplesin.' Reviewer 2 states 'This work contributes several important and interesting observations regarding the heterotolerance of non-growing Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa to the antimicrobial peptide tachyplesin.' Reviewer 3 describes it as 'This important study' that 'provides valuable insight into non genetic resistance mechanisms to AMPs and highlights inducible heterogeneity as a critical obstacle to peptide therapeutics.'

results.result: This study shows for the first time the upregulation of a range of MFS, ABC, and RND efflux pumps in a stationary phase subpopulation that exhibited low accumulation of tachyplesin with corresponding enhanced survival.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support this as a novel finding while noting that the mechanism requires further investigation. Reviewer 3 states 'The relevance of efflux for the "low accumulator" phenotype and its survival is convincingly demonstrated' through multiple lines of evidence including transcriptomics. However, the same reviewer notes 'Despite these advances, the contribution of efflux may require more direct evidence to further dissect whether efflux is necessary, sufficient, or contributory. The facts that the key low-efflux mutant still retains a small fraction of survivors and that the inhibitors used may cause other physiological changes leading to higher efflux are still unaccounted for.'

results.result: Low and high accumulators have similar forward and violet side scatter values, but high accumulators are significantly smaller than low accumulators in the microfluidics platform (p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss these morphological findings, but they are presented as part of the characterization data that supports the distinction between the two subpopulations. The lack of reviewer comment suggests implicit acceptance of these supporting observations.

results.result: Background and contextual claims about antimicrobial resistance, AMPs, tachyplesin properties, mechanisms of AMP action and resistance, efflux pumps, phenotypic resistance, and related literature findings.
results.evaluation: These are background claims supported by citations to published literature. Reviewers do not challenge any of these contextual claims, implicitly accepting them as established knowledge that frames the study. These claims provide the scientific rationale and context for the experimental work.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on bimodal accumulation patterns (C17-C29). Both evaluations find the flow cytometry data comprehensive and well-supported across multiple strains and species. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency and appropriate controls; peer reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding with all three reviewers confirming the bimodal distribution.

Strong agreement on differential localization findings (C30-C36). Both evaluations support the evidence distinguishing membrane-bound from intracellular peptide. OpenEval highlights multiple complementary methods and statistical rigor; peer reviewers note the added experiments 'substantially improved' the manuscript and 'strengthen the assertion' about localization differences. Peer review also addresses C37-C38 (morphological findings) which OpenEval covers separately.

Complete agreement on the link between accumulation, membrane integrity, and survival (C39-C45). Both evaluations find the evidence compelling with robust statistical analyses. OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic link through multiple independent assays; peer reviewers describe the demonstration as 'compelling' with strong correlation data between low accumulators and survivors.

Strong agreement on temporal dynamics showing induced response (C63-C66, C91). Both evaluations support the finding that low accumulation emerges after initial high accumulation. OpenEval emphasizes the kinetic data distinguishing induced from pre-existing phenotypes; peer reviewers explicitly note this as 'interesting' and important for demonstrating the phenotype is 'an induced response and not a pre-existing property.'

Agreement on transcriptomic findings (C46-C54) with shared interpretive caution. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical methods but acknowledges limitations about causation vs. consequence. Peer review (R5) supports the transcriptomic data while explicitly cautioning about the same limitation: 'challenging to interpret whether any differences seen between the two groups are causative for the observed accumulation pattern or if they are a consequence.' Both acknowledge authors' appropriate interpretation.

Agreement on lipidomic and additional transcriptomic findings (C55-C60). OpenEval finds the integration of transcriptomic and lipidomic data well-supported with appropriate citations. Peer review R5 addresses these claims as part of broader transcriptomic analysis, supporting the findings while noting interpretive limitations about causality.

Both evaluations express uncertainty about computational TF predictions (C61-C62). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are indirect computational predictions requiring experimental validation. Peer review R5 does not explicitly challenge these claims but groups them with transcriptomic findings that have interpretive limitations, implicitly supporting the cautious interpretation.

Strong agreement on genetic evidence for efflux systems (C67-C68, C90, C100). Both evaluations support the deletion mutant findings. OpenEval emphasizes the complete elimination of low accumulators in qseBC mutants as strong evidence; peer reviewers confirm the phenotype was 'nearly abrogated' and note 'the strength of the phenotype' while acknowledging remaining mechanistic questions about additional factors.

Agreement on efflux inhibitor findings (C70-C73, C102) with shared caveats. Both evaluations support the sertraline data showing prevention of low accumulator phenotype and enhanced efficacy. OpenEval notes the limitation about clinically achievable concentrations; peer reviewers support the finding as 'important basis for developing combination therapies' while cautioning about inhibitor specificity ('not perfectly selective').

Agreement on metabolic activity correlation (C74) with OpenEval expressing more caution. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting concerns about CCCP effects and need for validation with alternative assays. Peer review R8 supports the metabolic findings as 'important additions' without explicitly addressing the methodological concerns OpenEval raises about resorufin efflux artifacts.

Strong agreement on metabolic state and nutrient effects (C75-C78). Both evaluations support these findings as important. OpenEval emphasizes consistent effects across multiple conditions; peer reviewers explicitly praise the 'new data on nutrient supplementation' and note the findings are 'highly relevant also beyond the presented example of tachyplesin.'

Complete agreement on the central mechanistic model (C79-C80, C84-C85). Both evaluations strongly support the synthesis linking accumulation, localization, and survival. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative correlations; peer reviewers affirm the novelty and importance, with all three reviewers describing the study as 'important' and providing 'valuable insight' into non-genetic resistance mechanisms.

Agreement on novelty and significance (C84-C85, C89, C91). OpenEval supports the claim of first observation with comprehensive characterization. Peer review R9 affirms novelty and importance across all three reviewers. Peer review R10 addresses C89 specifically, supporting efflux relevance while noting the mechanism requires further investigation for direct evidence.

Agreement on efflux mechanism novelty (C89) with nuanced interpretation. OpenEval supports this as novel finding with comprehensive evidence. Peer review R10 states 'The relevance of efflux for the "low accumulator" phenotype and its survival is convincingly demonstrated' but notes 'the contribution of efflux may require more direct evidence to further dissect whether efflux is necessary, sufficient, or contributory.'

Implicit agreement on LPS modification mechanism (C94). OpenEval supports this finding with appropriate citations, noting direct measurement would strengthen conclusions. Peer review R12 does not explicitly discuss this claim but includes it among background/contextual claims that are implicitly accepted as part of the overall study framework.

Agreement on QseBC role (C99-C100) with OpenEval providing more detail. OpenEval emphasizes the striking elimination of low accumulators and notes potential pleiotropic effects. Peer review R6 confirms the qseBC mutant phenotype and notes 'its centrality for the tachyplesin response,' suggesting it 'may control additional as-of-yet unidentified factors.'

Peer review R12 includes C99 among background/contextual claims that frame the study. OpenEval R15 treats C99-C100 as primary findings about QseBC's role. This represents different organizational approaches rather than disagreement on the evidence itself.

Complete agreement on background and contextual claims (C1-C16, C23, C81-C88, C92-C93, C95-C98, C101, C103-C106). Both evaluations accept these as appropriately cited established literature. OpenEval notes they 'accurately represent prior work'; peer reviewers 'do not challenge any of these contextual claims, implicitly accepting them as established knowledge.'

Morphological observations (C37-C38) addressed differently. OpenEval includes these with localization findings in R2 as supporting evidence. Peer review R11 notes these claims are 'presented as part of the characterization data' with 'lack of reviewer comment suggests implicit acceptance' rather than explicit evaluation.
